Hmm, but the step goal is "design an experiment plan for the most promising direction." The most promising direction given the critique: a leakage-controlled head-to-head comparison of soft vs hard temporal handling. Let me design that.

Fields:
- title: "Leakage-controlled head-to-head evaluation of soft elapsed-time re-ranking versus hard validity-interval filtering on amended statutes"
- research_question
- hypothesis
- proposed_method
- baselines (strong and budget-matched): 
  - B1 semantic-only (BM25 and dense)
  - B2 hard validity-interval filter (as-of date; Prior et al. RAG-kNN style) + semantic ranking within filter
  - B3 hard future-mask only (TempRALM-style mask, no decay)
  - B4 recency-only ranker (latest version)
  - B5 TempRALM-style soft elapsed-time (semantic + decay)
  - B6 oracle in-force filter (upper bound)
- datasets: German statutory corpus with version timeline (from TUMLegalTech/temporal_bias + official consolidated statute versions); optionally EU/UK legislation (Chalkidis et al.) as transfer set.
- workloads: query regimes — current/post-amendment, historically anchored pre-amendment, multi-provision; plus a synthetic control set with timestamps permuted.
- metrics: version-selection accuracy@k (primary), Recall@k, MRR, nDCG@k, answer accuracy (LLM-as-judge validated), per-regime.
- ablations: decay shape (exponential/linear/step), lambda sweep, timestamp-shuffled control, date-randomized control, query-date-offset control, no-temporal (semantic only).
- controls: identical index, no re-embedding, matched top-k, fixed generator/prompt, tuned on held-out split.
- confounders addressed: label leakage (held-out tuning; timestamp-shuffled and version-id-permuted controls; report lambda sensitivity), regime mixing (stratified per-regime reporting), retriever-specificity (BM25 + 2 dense), generator sensitivity (2 LLMs), benchmark construct (manual audit of a sample; exclude items where gold could be matched without temporal cue).
- expected_outcomes: if soft decay adds value beyond hard filter, version-selection accuracy should improve over B3 and not be explained by shuffled-timestamp control; per-regime, expect gains on current queries and losses on historical ones unless lambda is regime-conditioned; expect hard filter B2 to dominate B5 if Prior et al.'s conclusion generalizes.
- failure_conditions (falsify hypothesis): soft-term gain disappears under held-out tuning or under timestamp-shuffled control (leakage explanation); or hard filter dominates soft term on both regimes and version-selection accuracy; or version-selection accuracy does not improve though answer accuracy does (decoupling → gains from generator, not retrieval); or soft term no better than recency-only latest-version baseline.
- reproducibility notes.

Designing the experiment plan that makes U007's confounder testable, then updating the uncertainty.

ablations: Temporal-term shape: exponential vs. linear vs. step (in-force indicator) decay
Temporal weight lambda swept over a fixed grid and reported as a sensitivity curve, not a single tuned value
Semantic-only retrieval with identical index and top-k (no temporal term at all)
Future-mask only (no decay), isolating the 'not-yet-in-force' effect from the 'recency' effect, matching TempRALM's masking step (arxiv:2401.13222)
Timestamp-shuffled control: gold-version timestamps randomly permuted across candidate versions while content is unchanged
Query-date offset control: query dates shifted by a fixed interval so that elapsed-time ordering no longer aligns with in-force ordering
Regime-conditioned lambda (separate weight for current vs. historically anchored queries) versus a single global lambda
baselines: Budget-matched semantic-only retrieval with the same index, chunking, top-k and generator: BM25 and a dense bi-encoder

Hard validity-interval filtering (as-of date extracted, retrieval restricted to versions in force at t_q), reimplementing Prior et al.'s RAG-kNN setting (arxiv:2605.23497); the primary strong baseline
Future-mask-only re-ranker (passages with version timestamp > t_q removed, no decay term) to match TempRALM's masking component (arxiv:2401.13222)
Recency-only ranker that always prefers the newest version, exposing recency bias
Oracle in-force filter using gold in-force intervals (upper bound, not a deployable system)
TempRALM-style soft score: semantic + lambda * f(|t_q - t_v|) without validity intervals (the idea's mechanism)
confounders_addressed: Timestamp label leakage: all hyperparameters tuned on a held-out question split disjoint from the test split; the timestamp-shuffled and query-date-offset controls must fail to reproduce any gain
Regime mixing: results reported stratified by query-date regime so current-version and historical questions cannot cancel out
Retriever-specific effects: the wrapper is evaluated on BM25 plus at least two dense encoders under matched budgets

Benchmark construct artifacts: a manually audited sample of items is excluded when the correct version can be identified without any temporal cue, and question-generation artifacts are inspected against the source statute
Generator effects: answer accuracy is measured with two different LLM judges/generators while retrieval metrics remain generator-independent
Hyperparameter overfitting to one lambda: the full sensitivity curve is reported and significance is assessed at the pre-registered lambda, not the argmax
datasets: Amended German statutory corpus with per-version effective dates, using the source provisions underlying the TUMLegalTech/temporal_bias benchmark (arxiv:2605.23497) and official consolidated statute versions
Held-out split of the 312 time-sensitive statutory QA pairs (arxiv:2605.23497), stratified by the three categories (Post-Cutoff Amendment, Pre-Amendment, Multi-Provision Pre-Amendment)
A transfer set of EU/UK amended legislation with version metadata (candidate source: Chalkidis et al., arxiv:2101.10726) to test jurisdiction transfer
Synthetic control instances with permuted version timestamps and shifted query dates, built from the same passages
input.expected_outcomes: If the soft temporal term adds genuine value, it should improve version-selection accuracy@k over future-mask-only (B3) and recency-only (B4), and the gain must vanish under the timestamp-shuffled control and persist under held-out tuning. On the basis of Prior et al., the most likely outcome is that hard validity filtering (B2) dominates the soft term overall, with the soft term showing partial benefit only when validity intervals are unavailable or noisy; a secondary likely outcome is regime-dependent behaviour, with gains on current queries and degradation on historically anchored ones unless lambda is regime-conditioned.
failure_conditions: The soft-term gain over semantic-only disappears when lambda is tuned on a held-out split, or is reproduced by the timestamp-shuffled control (leakage explanation confirmed, hypothesis falsified)
The hard validity filter matches or beats the soft term on version-selection accuracy in both regimes, leaving the soft term with no measurable contribution
Answer accuracy improves while version-selection accuracy does not, showing the gain comes from the generator rather than temporal retrieval
The soft term is no better than the recency-only newest-version baseline, showing it captures only recency bias
The soft term helps only on current/post-amendment questions while harming historically anchored ones, so no global lambda satisfies the stated research question
input.hardware: Experiments are retrieval- and API-bound rather than compute-bound. One workstation or a single modest GPU node for dense encoding of the statute corpus and local reranking is sufficient; if a local open-weight generator is used, one 24-40 GB GPU. No model training is required, consistent with the retrieval-agnostic, training-free claim.
metrics: Primary: version-selection accuracy@k (fraction of top-k retrieved passages whose version is in force at t_q)
Secondary retrieval: Recall@k, MRR, nDCG@k on gold passages
End-task: answer accuracy (exact match / F1 and LLM-as-judge correctness validated against a human-rated sample)
Reported stratified by query-date regime (current/post-amendment vs. historically anchored vs. multi-provision)
Delta over semantic-only, over future-mask-only, over recency-only, and over hard validity filtering, each with held-out tuning
input.proposed_method: A leakage-controlled, budget-matched head-to-head study on one fixed versioned statutory corpus and one shared index. Candidate passages from all versions are scored by a fixed retriever s(q,p); the method adds a soft elapsed-time term lambda * f(|t_q - t_v(p)|) where f is exponential, linear or step-shaped, and t_q is the query's target date. All temporal hyperparameters are tuned on a held-out question split and never on the test split. The same index, chunking, top-k and generator are reused across arms so that only the ranking rule changes. Results are reported per query-date regime and accompanied by timestamp-shuffled and query-date-offset control runs. Two interval-aware variants are also tested: a step decay equal to an in-force indicator, and a validity-interval-aware term that uses effective/expiry dates rather than elapsed time.
input.reproducibility_notes: The benchmark data underlying arxiv:2605.23497 is public (github.com/TUMLegalTech/temporal_bias; root files 'Prompts' and 'qa_set.xlsx'), but that repository contains no code for the retrieval or ranking pipeline and its README is empty, so the retrieval experiment must be implemented from scratch. TempRALM has no public repository (search_github for 'TempRALM' returned nothing), and the TaxFlow system (doi:10.1080/08839514.2026.2626097) provides no code in its abstract. Because no open implementation of the scoring wrapper on regulatory corpora exists and assembling the versioned corpus, in-force intervals and retrieval pipeline is not a small or safe automated run, no execution spec is attached; the experiment requires human setup. All random seeds, exact statute version snapshots, embedding model names and revision hashes, date-extraction rules, top-k values, lambda grids and judge prompts must be logged. Corpus version snapshots must be archived because legislation changes, making exact reproduction otherwise impossible.
input.research_question: When the soft elapsed-time term and hard validity-interval filtering are compared under identical conditions and leakage-controlled tuning, does the soft term improve version-selection and answer accuracy on amended regulatory texts - or is any apparent gain an artifact of tuning the temporal weight lambda against gold-version-anchored questions?
input.title: Leakage-controlled head-to-head evaluation of soft elapsed-time re-ranking versus hard validity-interval filtering on amended statutory corpora
input.hypothesis: Under held-out hyperparameter tuning and timestamp-shuffled / date-offset controls, the soft elapsed-time temporal term does not, by itself, produce a version-selection accuracy gain over future-mask-only and recency-only baselines; hard validity-interval filtering matches or outperforms it, and any soft-term benefit is confined to settings where validity intervals are unavailable or noisy.
workloads: Current/post-amendment queries whose correct version is the newest or a recent one
Historically anchored pre-amendment queries whose correct version is an older, superseded one
Multi-provision queries spanning several paragraphs with mixed version applicability
Control workloads with permuted version timestamps and with query dates shifted by a fixed offset
Sparse (BM25) and dense retrieval workloads evaluated under identical passage segmentation and top-k budgets

input.description: The idea assumes one global temporal weighting rule. Prior et al. show current-version and historical-version questions pull in opposite directions (recency helps post-cutoff queries but causes recency bias on historically anchored ones). If that holds under the planned experiment, the defensible contribution becomes a regime-conditioned or validity-interval-aware temporal score rather than a single elapsed-time decay, which would require changing the mechanism rather than only tuning lambda.
input.question: If current-version and historically anchored queries require opposite temporal weighting, must the temporal component be conditioned on the query-date regime (or replaced by a validity-interval-aware score) rather than using a single elapsed-time decay?
input.rationale: Determines whether the surviving contribution is a tuned scalar decay or a different mechanism, which changes the research direction and the novelty framing.

input.resolution: No retrieved evidence tests this directly: TempRALM tunes a scaling factor without a leakage analysis (arxiv:2401.13222) and Prior et al. do not report lambda-style tuning or retrieval-layer metrics (arxiv:2605.23497). The uncertainty therefore cannot be settled from literature and must be settled by experiment. An experiment plan has been recorded that specifies the controls required to distinguish leakage from genuine temporal skill: held-out tuning of lambda, a timestamp-shuffled control, a query-date-offset control, a future-mask-only ablation, a recency-only baseline, and per-regime reporting. Until those runs exist and are verified, the confounder remains open.
